⚖️ The Ledger

Runs made with the bat, minus runs conceded with the ball — each player's net run balance for the club. Runs scored count for you; runs conceded count against. Genuine two-way players only (bowled 50+ overs and batted 10+ innings). A bit of fun, not a verdict — the deep-red figures belong to the frontline bowlers, in the red only because they send down over after over; the wickets column is what they got for it.

🏏 The Batsman's Ledger

The batsman's mirror of the bowler's ledger: your runs, minus your share of the runs the team conceded while you were among the batters. Balls-faced isn't on the old cards, so the concession is shared equally across the XI that batted each game — everyone carries a slice of what leaked, and the question is whether the bat covered it. Totals reward the run-machines; the per-game view (minimum 25 games) strips longevity out.

🎳 The Bowler's Ledger

A bowler's net worth to the club: credit each a share of the team's runs in proportion to the overs they sent down, then subtract what they conceded — the workhorses earning a fair claim on the runs the batters made while they toiled. Every share adds up to exactly the club's runs, so it's a fair carve-up of the whole run difference by workload. Totals reward the big engines; the per-game view (minimum 25 games) strips longevity out to find the real difference-makers.

🧤 The Keeper's Ledger

The gloveman's balance: runs made in the matches they kept, minus byes conceded behind the stumps — bat and gloves judged over the very same games. Byes aren't logged against a keeper, so each innings' byes are charged to whoever was keeping, inferred from stumpings and catches as the catch boards are (about three-quarters can be pinned down; keeper-unknown innings are left out). The batting keepers stay in credit; the specialist glovemen who leaked more than they made slip into the red.
